pr.title: match lowering: expand or-candidates mixed with candidates above
pr.description:
This PR tweaks match lowering of or-patterns. Consider this:
```rust
match (x, y) {
    (1, true) => 1,
    (2, false) => 2,
    (1 | 2, true | false) => 3,
    (3 | 4, true | false) => 4,
    _ => 5,
}
```
One might hope that this can be compiled to a single `SwitchInt` on `x` followed by some boolean checks. Before this PR, we compile this to 3 `SwitchInt`s on `x`, because an arm that contains more than one or-pattern was compiled on its own. This PR groups branch `3` with the two branches above, getting us down to 2 `SwitchInt`s on `x`.

We can't in general expand or-patterns freely, because this interacts poorly with another optimization we do: or-pattern simplification. When an or-pattern doesn't involve bindings, we branch the success paths of all its alternatives to the same block. The drawback is that in a case like: 
```rust
match (1, true) {
    (1 | 2, false) => unreachable!(),
    (2, _) => unreachable!(),
    _ => {}
}
```
if we used a single `SwitchInt`, by the time we test `false` we don't know whether we came from the `1` case or the `2` case, so we don't know where to go if `false` doesn't match.

Hence the limitation: we can process or-pattern alternatives alongside candidates that precede it, but not candidates that follow it. (Unless the or-pattern is the only remaining match pair of its candidate, in which case we can process it alongside whatever).

This PR allows the processing of or-pattern alternatives alongside candidates that precede it. One benefit is that we now process or-patterns in a single place in `mod.rs`.

analysis.summary: rustc_mir_build match lowering now expands leading or-pattern candidates only up to the first candidate that has additional match pairs, then processes expanded candidates before the remaining candidates. This groups or-arms with preceding candidates, reducing repeated SwitchInt tests (the PR example goes from 3 to 2 SwitchInts on x) while preserving correct failure and guard paths that or-pattern simplification would otherwise confuse.
analysis.originalLogic: Before this PR, match_candidates only split a candidate when its sole match pair was an Or, using `if let [MatchPair { test_case: TestCase::Or { .. }, .. }] = &*candidate.match_pairs`. Candidates with additional match pairs were handled later by `test_candidates_with_or` / `test_or_pattern`. As the PR description says: "Before this PR, we compile this to 3 `SwitchInt`s on `x`, because an arm that contains more than one or-pattern was compiled on its own." Also, `Candidate::otherwise_block` was documented/used only for guards: "If the guard is `false` then branch to `otherwise_block`," and `select_matched_candidate` set it only under `if candidate.has_guard`.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: The unsafe expansion is to freely expand or-patterns and keep processing candidates that follow them in the same candidate set. Or-pattern simplification branches the success paths of all alternatives to the same block; then a later failed test no longer knows which alternative succeeded, so its failure edge cannot be routed to the correct remaining candidate. The PR states this directly for `match (1, true) { (1 | 2, false) => ..., (2, _) => ..., _ => ... }`: "if we used a single `SwitchInt`, by the time we test `false` we don't know whether we came from the `1` case or the `2` case, so we don't know where to go if `false` doesn't match." A related incorrect skip is taken in `finalize_or_candidate`: when a subcandidate has a guard, "`leaf_candidate.otherwise_block` can be reached by guard failure as well, so we" cannot skip testing the next alternative. Thus the correct rule is the source-backed limitation: "we can process or-pattern alternatives alongside candidates that precede it, but not candidates that follow it. (Unless the or-pattern is the only remaining match pair of its candidate, in which case we can process it alongside whatever)."
analysis.inputDomain: Rust match expressions lowered by rustc_mir_build when candidates contain or-patterns (`|`), including nested tuple scrutinees and multiple or-patterns in one arm, with or without guards. Concrete shapes in the patch include `((i32, i32), i32)` with bindings, `(i32, bool)`, `(bool, bool, bool)`, `(bool, bool)`, and integer/bool fields suitable for `SwitchInt`. The distinction that matters is whether a candidate's leading match pair is `TestCase::Or` and whether that candidate has only that one remaining match pair or additional match pairs after it.
analysis.trigger: A candidate's `match_pairs` starts with `MatchPair { test_case: TestCase::Or { .. }, .. }`. If it is the candidate's only remaining match pair, it may be expanded freely. If it has more match pairs, expansion may include that candidate but must stop before any following candidates: the fixed code sets `expand_until = i + 1` and breaks when `candidate.match_pairs.len() > 1`, then splits with `let (candidates_to_expand, remaining_candidates) = candidates.split_at_mut(expand_until);`. The optimization opportunity is an arm with multiple or-patterns that previously was processed on its own instead of alongside preceding candidates.
preconditions: The first match pair of a candidate is an or-pattern.
A candidate with more than one remaining match pair bounds the expansion set; candidates after it must remain in `remaining_candidates` and be processed from `remainder_start`.
After expansion, each expanded candidate is finalized with `finalize_or_candidate`, which merges trivial subcandidates and then appends leftover match pairs to every leaf.
For leftover match pairs, the failure target is the last leaf's `otherwise_block`; if a leaf has a guard, use that leaf's own `otherwise_block` instead, because guard failure can reach it.
`select_matched_candidate` must set `candidate.otherwise_block` for every matched candidate, not only guarded ones, since a nested candidate can also fail to match.
`merge_trivial_subcandidates` refuses to merge when the candidate has a guard or when any subcandidate has non-empty `extra_data` (bindings).
pitfalls: Do not treat fewer SwitchInts as sufficient: moving failure edges across an or-pattern simplification can select the wrong next candidate.
Do not expand an or-pattern candidate together with candidates that follow it unless the or-pattern is that candidate's only remaining match pair.
Do not skip trying the second or-alternative when a guard is present; unlike the no-guard case, the failure block may be reached by guard failure.
Dummy or-patterns such as `_ | _` can still force a guard to run multiple times, so guard side effects/counts are observable.
Do not naively sort identical tested values together and share failure paths; the new `simplification_subtleties` test uses `(1 | 2, false | false)` followed by `(2, _)` specifically to catch this.
The `otherwise_block` is now needed for all selected candidates, so retaining the old guard-only assignment would lose the pre-binding failure path.
analysis.testStrategy: Use `tests/mir-opt/or_pattern.rs` with `// EMIT_MIR or_pattern.shortcut_second_or.SimplifyCfg-initial.after.mir` and `// EMIT_MIR or_pattern.single_switchint.SimplifyCfg-initial.after.mir` to inspect post-`SimplifyCfg-initial` MIR. For `single_switchint`, check the MIR uses two `SwitchInt`s on `_2.0` rather than one per or-arm. For `shortcut_second_or`, check that after matching `0`, failing `2 | 3` skips trying `(1, 2 | 3)` as the test comment requests. Add run-pass behavioral tests for failure routing and guard counts: `simplification_subtleties.rs` (`(1 | 2, false | false)` then `(2, _)`), `search_with_dummy` expecting guard counts 1, 3, 5, 7, `issue-70413-no-unreachable-pat-and-guard.rs` as run-pass, and the added `or_at(Err(34)) == 134` case in `bindings-runpass-2.rs`. No compiler was built here, so these are inspection/test-construction strategies, not reproduced executions.
